paras: The attempted lynching of Henry Purnell took place near Tuckerman, Arkansas, on June 20, 1881, when a posse of citizens that had hunted him all day for an alleged rape captured him in the woods and nearly hanged him. Purnell, a farm hand of about sixty, was instead jailed, pleaded guilty before a justice the next morning, and was held under guard amid threats of lynching. The case reached papers from Memphis to Idaho through an Arkansas Gazette special and a shorter wire brief, none of which stated anyone's race.

Purnell had worked for some time as a farm hand for Maurice Crabb near Tuckerman and had been "received into his family." Crabb's seven-year-old daughter carried fresh water to the men in the field two or three times a day.

According to the Gazette's correspondent, on Monday afternoon Crabb went back toward the house, returned to the field, and said he surprised Purnell assaulting the girl. Purnell ran, and Crabb raised the alarm among his neighbors, after which "a large number of citizens" set out after him. After searching all day they captured him late in the evening in thick woods about four miles from the farm.

The fullest text of the dispatch, printed in the Memphis Daily Appeal, said that "with difficulty" he was saved "from hanging at the hands of the furious posse" and was put in jail instead. It does not say who intervened.

The next morning Purnell was taken before Justice W. H. Jack of Jacksonport, pleaded guilty to rape, and was remanded to jail. The Appeal's text added that "very menacing threats of lynching" had been made, and a wire brief reported him held "under a heavy guard." No report of a trial, sentence or later lynching appears in the coverage.

The Memphis Daily Appeal of June 23 ran the Gazette special under decks calling Purnell "A Gray-Headed Old Wretch" and a "Libidinous Old Wretch Who Should Have Been [Hanged]," and its text called him "the brutish old man." The same day the St. Paul Daily Globe printed a shorter version as "Brutal Deed," naming him "H. Parnell" and leaving out the near-hanging and the threats. Western papers carried only a two-sentence telegraphic item, in the Silver State of Unionville, Nevada, on June 25 and in the Idaho Semi-Weekly World on July 1.
None of the papers identified Purnell, the Crabbs or the posse by race.

chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A posse of citizens that captured Purnell after a manhunt is reported to have nearly hanged him before he was jailed, and lynching threats followed (A1); he was not killed (A1, A2, A3).

A 'furious posse' drawn from 'a large number of citizens' is reported to have tried to hang Purnell over a rape accusation, but he was saved and jailed (A1, A2); no one was killed, so this was an attempted lynching, not a lynching.

The accusation, capture and jailing appear in three papers (A1, A2, A3), but all derive from one Arkansas Gazette special, and the near-hanging and lynching threats appear only in the Memphis text (A1).

info: Alleged assault and the pursuit and capture on Monday afternoon and evening, 'day before yesterday' from a June 22 dispatch, i.e. June 20, 1881; guilty plea before a justice the next morning (June 21).
Crabb's farm near Tuckerman, Ark.; capture and near-hanging in thick woods about four miles from the scene.
Henry Purnell ('H. Parnell' in one text), about sixty, a farm hand in Crabb's employ; race not stated in any article.
Accused of raping the seven-year-old daughter of his employer, Maurice ('Manrice') Crabb, who said he surprised him in the act.
A posse of 'a large number of citizens' who pursued and captured him; none named.
Pleaded guilty to rape before Justice W. H. Jack of Jacksonport and was remanded to jail; no later report of a trial, sentence or lynching was found.
